title: Mystery-call your restaurant and check the basics
seoTitle: Mystery-call your restaurant for missed calls | ROAL
description: Use a mystery shopper call to spot missed calls, weak greetings, and slow order taking. Get a simple script, checklist, and fixes.
question: How do I mystery-call my own restaurant and find out what happens when customers call?
answer: Call your restaurant like a customer and listen for what happens before, during, and after the greeting. Check whether the phone gets answered quickly, whether the team can take orders and questions clearly, and whether missed calls go to voicemail or nowhere at all. A short mystery shopper call restaurant test can show you where calls are being lost and what to fix first.
summary: You can mystery-call your own restaurant, score the call, and fix the weak spots that cost orders.
intro:
A mystery shopper call restaurant check is just you calling your own store like a customer. It shows you whether the phone gets answered, whether the greeting sounds clean, and whether the staff can take an order without confusion.

Do it once during a calm hour and once during a rush. Then compare what you heard. If the call is rough, tools like ROAL can answer routine calls, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and hand tricky questions to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: What should I listen for on my own call?
sections.body:
Start with the basics. A mystery call is not about being picky. It is about hearing the same experience your customers hear when they want food fast.

Use this simple scorecard. Give each item a yes or no.

| Check | What to listen for |
|---|---|
| Speed | Did someone answer before the caller gave up? |
| Greeting | Did they say the restaurant name clearly? |
| Order taking | Could they repeat items, sizes, modifiers, and notes correctly? |
| Menu questions | Could they answer hours, address, parking, and common menu questions? |
| Ready time | Did they quote a clear pickup time? |
| Follow-through | Did they confirm the order back before hanging up? |

Try a real restaurant example. Say you sell a $28 pickup order: one large pie, one salad, and a drink. Ask for a simple modifier, like extra sauce or no onions. Then ask one common question, like parking or closing time. If the person sounds rushed or unsure, that is a call worth fixing.

A good phone script line sounds like this: "Thanks for calling. This is [restaurant name]. What can I get started for you?" If your team cannot say something that clear every time, write it down and train it.

sections.h2: How do I run the mystery call without making it weird?
sections.body:
Keep it simple and private. You do not need a big plan. You need one clean call and honest notes.

1. Pick the right time.
   - Do one call during a slow period.
   - Do one call during lunch or dinner rush.
2. Use a normal phone number.
   - Call from your own cell or another line.
   - Do not use a blocked or hidden number.
3. Act like a real customer.
   - Order one or two items.
   - Ask one question about hours, delivery area, or parking.
4. Write down what happened.
   - Time to answer.
   - Name used on the call.
   - Whether the order was repeated back.
   - Whether the caller’s phone number was collected.
5. Compare the two calls.
   - Slow hour versus busy hour often tells two different stories.

If you want a repeatable test, use the same script every time. For example: "Hi, I’d like to place a pickup order. Can I get a large pepperoni with light cheese, one side salad, and extra dressing? What time would that be ready?" If your staff answers well once but misses it later, the issue may be rush-hour coverage, not skill.

ROAL is useful here because owners can test-call it right in the browser from their website or Google Maps listing before going live. That makes it easy to compare how a phone host handles the same questions over and over, without waiting for a real customer complaint.

sections.h2: What problems does a mystery call usually reveal?
sections.body:
Most restaurants do not have one phone problem. They have a stack of small ones. A mystery call helps you see which one is costing you the most.

Here are the common patterns:

- The phone rings too long before anyone picks up.
- The greeting is vague, like "hello" instead of the restaurant name.
- The staff sounds distracted and misses the caller’s name or phone number.
- The order is taken, but the item details are incomplete.
- The caller is put on hold and never comes back.
- Hours, address, or parking questions are answered incorrectly.
- Allergy-sensitive or complaint calls are handled without a clear handoff.

A useful way to think about it: if a caller is trying to spend $24, $36, or $52 with you, every extra step can lose the sale. For a $30 average order, plug in your own number and ask yourself how many calls you would need to make up one lost order. That is often where the pain shows up.

You can also use the mystery call to test how your current setup handles forwarding. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off. Some mobile carriers use different codes for unanswered or busy calls, and business VoIP systems usually set it in a web portal. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. A missed forwarded call is still a missed call.

sections.h2: How do I turn call problems into a simple fix list?
sections.body:
Do not leave the mystery call as a vague feeling. Turn it into a fix list with owners and due dates. Keep it practical and short.

| Problem heard on the call | Fix to make | Who owns it |
|---|---|---|
| No greeting script | Post a one-line script near the phone | Manager |
| Wrong ready-time quote | Set a standard time range for common orders | Kitchen lead |
| Forgotten phone number | Add a name-and-number step to the script | Front counter |
| Menu confusion | Update the menu board or phone FAQ | Owner |
| Busy-hour missed calls | Forward busy or unanswered calls | Owner or manager |

A simple script can help right away:
"I can help with that. Let me repeat your order back so we get it right."

If you are short-staffed, that line matters a lot. It slows the call just enough to reduce mistakes without making the caller feel brushed off.

It can also hand off catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That means your team spends less time on repetitive calls and more time on the guests in front of them.

sections.h2: How should I test the cost of missed calls against my current setup?
sections.body:
A mystery call is more useful when you connect it to dollars. You do not need a perfect model. You just need a rough one that matches your shop.

Use this quick example and swap in your own numbers:

- Say your average phone order is $28.
- Say 3 missed calls in a busy night would have become orders.
- That is $84 in lost sales for one shift.

Now compare that to the cost of your current answer setup. Third-party delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call.

Use this quick comparison checklist:
- What do you pay when no order comes in?
- What happens when calls spike during dinner?
- Do you pay for test calls?
- Does the system help with pickup orders from your menu, or just answer questions?

If your mystery call shows that the phone is often the weak link, it may be worth comparing costs before another busy weekend.

sections.h2: What should I do after the test call?
sections.body:
After the call, do three things right away.

1. Write the score.
   - Answered quickly or not.
   - Clear greeting or not.
   - Order taken cleanly or not.
2. Fix the easiest issue first.
   - Script.
   - Forwarding.
   - Hours or menu info.
3. Retest the same script.
   - Use the same order.
   - Use the same question.
   - Compare the result.

If you want a simple owner checklist, use this:
- [ ] The phone is answered during rush hour.
- [ ] The restaurant name is said clearly.
- [ ] The caller’s order is repeated back.
- [ ] The caller’s name and phone are collected.
- [ ] Hours, address, and parking are correct.
- [ ] Allergy or manager requests are handed to staff.
- [ ] The kitchen gets a clean ticket, not a messy note.

For many owners, the real win is not the mystery call itself. It is the habit. You hear your own phone the way customers do, then you clean up the weak spots before they turn into bad reviews or lost pickup sales. You can also keep a short log in your dashboard. ROAL includes call history with transcripts and recordings, plus a kitchen screen with live tickets, menu editing, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That gives you something to compare against the mystery call later.

sections.h2: How can I make mystery calls part of weekly management?
sections.body:
Do the test on a schedule, not only when something goes wrong. A short weekly call check is enough for many independent restaurants.

A simple routine:
- Monday: slow-hour test call.
- Friday: rush-hour test call.
- After any menu change: test the top sellers.
- After a forwarding change: test again from a mobile phone.

Keep the script the same for all tests. That way, you can compare results over time. For example, use the same order every week: one large pizza, one side, one drink, and one question about pickup time. If the answer changes, you will know exactly what changed.

Mystery calling your own restaurant is not about catching people doing something wrong. It is about hearing the truth. If the truth is that your team is doing fine, great. If the truth is that the phone is hurting orders, you now know where to focus. If you want a deeper look at phone behavior, ROAL’s blog also covers [rush-hour phone orders](/use-cases/rush-hour) and [short-staffed shifts](/use-cases/short-staffed).

takeaways: A mystery shopper call restaurant test shows you the real customer experience on the phone.
Use the same script each time so you can compare slow hours and rush hours.
Write down greeting, order accuracy, ready time, and handoff quality.
Turn the call into a fix list: script, forwarding, menu info, and staff handoff.
If routine calls are the problem, an AI phone host like ROAL can handle them and send clean kitchen tickets.

faq.q: How do I mystery-call my own restaurant without sounding fake?
faq.a: Use a normal phone number and a short, real order. Ask for one common item, one modifier, and one question about hours, parking, or pickup time. Keep your notes on how the call feels, how long it takes to answer, and whether the staff repeats the order back correctly.

faq.q: What should a good restaurant phone greeting sound like?
faq.a: It should be short, clear, and repeatable. A good example is: "Thanks for calling [restaurant name]. What can I get started for you?" That greeting tells the caller they reached the right place and makes it easier to move into the order quickly.

faq.q: What if my staff answers the phone but gets the order wrong?
faq.a: That usually means the problem is the call flow, not just the people. Add a simple repeat-back step for items, sizes, modifiers, and notes. If the rush makes that hard, an AI phone host can take routine pickup and delivery orders from your live menu and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: How do I know whether I should forward calls after a mystery test?
faq.a: If the phone rings too long, goes unanswered, or gets missed during busy periods, forwarding is worth testing. The exact code depends on your carrier or phone system, and it can be set differently for all calls, unanswered calls, or busy calls. Always confirm with your carrier and make a test call after you change it.
